source: Canadian National Autism Foundation, cnaf.net/provinceres.html; each entry checked on its own website

entries.name: AIDE Canada (Autism and/or Intellectual Disability Knowledge Exchange Network)
entries.description: A national online network, funded by the Public Health Agency of Canada, that connects autistic people, people with intellectual disabilities, families and professionals with evidence-informed resources. It offers articles, toolkits and courses, a free lending library, a map for locating programs, and live chat with staff who help people find resources.
entries.cost_note: Free community member accounts for borrowing library books and taking courses; the library is free.
entries.evidence: At its core, the Autism and/or Intellectual Disability Knowledge Exchange Network (AIDE Canada) is a tool to connect members of our community to the information and resources that they need.
entries.notes: CNAF lists AIDE Canada's 'Understanding Consent and Capacity Rules in Canada' toolkit (a document, still online) under Legal Help on its Alberta page; this entry is the organisation itself. Administered by the Pacific Autism Family Network Foundation; live chat runs 9am AST to 5pm PST, Monday to Friday.

entries.name: AIDE Canada (Autism and/or Intellectual Disability Knowledge Exchange Network)
entries.description: A national online hub of free resources for autistic people, people with intellectual disabilities and their families, with articles, toolkits, courses, videos, webinars and a free lending library open to everyone in Canada. Staff can help people find resources by live chat or email form.
entries.cost_note: The site says all of its resources are free.
entries.evidence: AIDE Canada is a tool to connect members of the autism, neurodiverse, and/or intellectual disability (ID) communities to the information and resources that they need.
entries.notes: CNAF's BC and Yukon pages link to several AIDE Canada toolkits and guides (consent and capacity toolkit, under-18 funding guide, NWT 18+ funding guide, school supports toolkit); the organisation is listed once here. Funded by the Public Health Agency of Canada and administered by the Pacific Autism Family Network Foundation.

entries.name: Disability Credit Canada
entries.description: A disability benefits firm that helps people in every province apply for the Disability Tax Credit, CPP disability benefits and long-term disability benefits, including for a child or spouse. It offers a free assessment, works on a no-win, no-fee basis, and publishes free guides for people who want to apply themselves.
entries.cost_note: Free assessment; "No-Win No-Fee", so a fee is charged only if the claim succeeds (the amount is not stated on the pages checked).
entries.evidence: We Offer a NO WIN – NO FEE Service and Provide Free, Comprehensive Information for Those Who Want to Apply Themselves.
entries.notes: A private, fee-charging representation service, not a government program; the Disability Tax Credit can also be applied for directly with the CRA (see disability-tax-credit). Office in Toronto (3701 Chesswood Drive). CNAF lists it twice (under 'Advocates about Disability Tax Credit' and under student scholarships); its scholarship is a separate entry.

entries.name: DCCI Scholarship for Canadian Students with Disabilities (Disability Credit Canada)
entries.description: An annual $1,000 scholarship toward tuition for a Canadian high school student with a documented disability who is going on to post-secondary studies in health care, criminal justice, or community and social services at an accredited Canadian institution. Students apply online, uploading their documents and an essay as one PDF.
entries.cost_note: A $1,000 award; the page does not mention an application fee.
entries.evidence: The annual scholarship winner will be awarded $1,000 towards their tuition to an accredited Canadian post-secondary institution.
entries.notes: Run by Disability Credit Canada, a private benefits firm. The page announces a 2026 winner and lists winners from 2019 to 2025, but its eligibility text still refers to the 2025/2026 academic year and no deadline is shown.

entries.name: 211 Canada
entries.description: A free, confidential helpline and website that connects people to government and community health and social services near them, such as help with food, housing, health care and employment. In most of Canada it can be reached 24 hours a day by phone, chat, text and web, in more than 150 languages.
entries.cost_note: The site says 211 is a free and confidential service.
entries.evidence: 211 is Canada’s primary source of information for government and community-based, non-clinical health and social services.
entries.notes: CNAF's link http://www.211.ca/ redirects to 211.ca. The site links to each province's or territory's 211 provider; service is run by United Way Centraide Canada and a national network of 211 providers. 211 Ontario is already in scripts/data/services/newcomers.json as 211-ontario.

entries.name: Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA)
entries.description: A national civil liberties and human rights charity that works on law reform, systemic advocacy and public education, including on disability equality. It does not give individual legal advice or representation, but people can report a civil liberties concern and use its know-your-rights guides and province-by-province legal resources referral sheet.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention cost.
entries.evidence: CCLA actively stands up to power by fighting against rights violations, abuse of police powers, inequality, and discrimination.
entries.notes: CNAF lists it under 'Legal Help', but the contact page says CCLA is a law reform organization that cannot provide individual legal representation or specific legal advice. Main phone and Toronto mailing address (400-124 Merton Street) from the contact page. The site refused the first fetch (403) but loaded on retry.

entries.name: Canadian Art Therapy Association (CATA)
entries.description: The national non-profit professional association for art therapists in Canada. Its website has a public directory of professional and registered CATA members that can be searched by location or keyword to find an art therapist, and explains what art therapy is.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention what art therapists charge.
entries.evidence: Looking for an art therapist? Search our directory of Professional and Registered CATA member by location or keyword to find the right art therapist for you.
entries.notes: CNAF's link http://canadianarttherapy.org/ redirects here. CNAF also used this same link for the Canadian Therapeutic Recreation Association (see unverified). The only address on the site is a PO box in Parksville, BC; the directory loads in an embedded frame.

entries.name: Canada Pension Plan (CPP) disability benefits
entries.description: A monthly payment for people over 18 and under 65 who have paid into the Canada Pension Plan and cannot work at any job on a regular basis because of a long-term mental or physical disability. You usually need CPP contributions in 4 of the 6 years before the disability stopped you working (or 3 of 6 with at least 25 years of contributions), and you must apply.
entries.cost_note: Federal benefit; the pages do not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: A Canada Pension Plan (CPP) disability benefit is a monthly payment that you could receive if you are over 18 and under 65 years old and unable to work because of a disability.
entries.notes: CNAF lists it twice: the eligibility page under 'Benefits', and an old servicecanada.gc.ca link (now landing on the general Service Canada page) under 'Services for People with Disabilities'. The 2026 maximum is $1,741.20 a month. Phone from the Contact Canada Pension Plan page; pages dated October 2026.

entries.name: Canada Pension Plan (CPP) children's benefits
entries.description: Monthly payments for the dependent children of a parent who receives a CPP disability benefit, or of a CPP contributor who has died. A child qualifies if under 18, or 18 to 25 and attending a recognized school or university full-time or part-time.
entries.cost_note: Federal benefit; the pages do not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: The Canada Pension Plan (CPP) children's benefits provide monthly payments to the dependent children of disabled or deceased CPP contributors.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old servicecanada.gc.ca page; that now lands on the general Service Canada page. The current canada.ca page is dated 2026-09-10. This benefit depends on the parent's CPP disability benefit or death; it is not paid for a child's own disability (see child-disability-benefit).

entries.name: Vocational Rehabilitation Program for Canada Pension Plan disability benefits recipients
entries.description: A voluntary program that helps people who receive a Canada Pension Plan disability benefit return to work, with employment counselling, an individual return-to-work plan, help with retraining costs and job-search support. People keep receiving their CPP disability benefit while they take part.
entries.cost_note: The page says the CPP may cover the costs of upgrading or retraining; it does not mention any fee.
entries.evidence: The Disability Vocational Rehabilitation Program is a voluntary program that helps Canada Pension Plan (CPP) disability benefit recipients return to work.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old servicecanada.gc.ca page; that now lands on the general Service Canada page. The current canada.ca page is dated 2025-11-04. Only for people already receiving CPP disability benefits; to take part, contact the Canada Pension Plan (phone from the Contact Canada Pension Plan page).

entries.name: Canada Student Grant for Services and Equipment – Students with Disabilities
entries.description: A federal grant of up to $20,000 per school year for post-secondary students with a disability who have financial need and need education-related services or equipment. Students apply with their provincial or territorial student aid application, sending proof of disability, written confirmation of the need from a qualified person and the cost of the services or equipment.
entries.cost_note: Federal grant; the page does not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: If you need education-related services or equipment, apply for the Canada Student Grant for Services and Equipment – Students with Disabilities.
entries.notes: CNAF lists it twice: this canada.ca page, and an old servicecanada.gc.ca link that now lands on the general Service Canada page. The page is dated 2022-08-02 but is still the current canada.ca page. Ontario students apply for it together with the Ontario BSWD (see ontario-bursary-students-with-disabilities).

entries.name: Canada Student Grant for Students with Disabilities
entries.description: A federal grant for post-secondary students with a disability who have financial need, available for each year of study; until the end of the 2026 to 2027 school year it is $2,800 a year. Students apply at the same time as they apply for student aid with their province or territory.
entries.cost_note: Federal grant; the page does not mention any fee to apply.
entries.evidence: This grant is available to students with disabilities for each year of study.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old servicecanada.gc.ca page ('Grant for Students with Permanent Disabilities'); that now lands on the general Service Canada page. Not available to students from the Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Quebec, which have their own programs. CNAF's 'seven things to remember' tips link to the general Canada Student Grants and Loans page, where students apply through their province or territory.

entries.name: Severe Permanent Disability Benefit (Canada Student Loans)
entries.description: Lets people with a severe permanent disability who cannot repay their Canada Student Loans apply to have the debt cancelled. The disability must prevent substantially gainful work and last for life; applicants mail an application form and a medical report completed by a doctor or nurse.
entries.cost_note: The page says the program does not reimburse any fee charged for completing the medical report form.
entries.evidence: Borrowers with a severe permanent disability who are unable to repay their Canada Student Loans may be eligible to have their debt cancelled through the Severe Permanent Disability Benefit.
entries.notes: CNAF lists it twice (under student grants and under Services for People with Disabilities); its old servicecanada.gc.ca link now lands on the general Service Canada page, and its other link is this current page (dated 2026-06-02). After receiving it, a person cannot get further Canada Student Grants or Loans. Phone is the National Student Loans Service Centre.

entries.name: Federal excise gasoline tax refund program
entries.description: A Canada Revenue Agency refund of part of the federal excise tax on gasoline for people with a permanent mobility impairment who cannot safely use public transportation. A qualified medical practitioner must certify the impairment, and people apply with Form XE8.
entries.cost_note: Federal tax refund; the page does not mention any fee.
entries.evidence: If you have a permanent mobility impairment and cannot safely use public transportation, you can ask for a refund of part of the federal excise tax on the gasoline you buy.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old servicecanada.gc.ca page; that now lands on the general Service Canada page. The CRA page (dated 2025-01-21) shows the refund is still offered. Only for permanent mobility impairments.

entries.name: Literature for the Blind (Canada Post)
entries.description: A free Canada Post service for mailing specific items used by people who are blind or visually impaired, within set size and weight limits. Eligible items can also go by Registered Mail or Xpresspost within Canada at no charge.
entries.cost_note: The page says it is a free service, including Registered Mail or Xpresspost in Canada.
entries.evidence: Literature for the Blind is a free service we offer that allows you to mail specific items used by visually impaired people.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old servicecanada.gc.ca page; that now lands on the general Service Canada page. An archived 2014 copy shows the old page pointed to Canada Post; Canada Post's current page shows the service is still offered. For blind or visually impaired people only.

entries.name: Assisted Living Program (Indigenous Services Canada)
entries.description: Funds non-medical social support services for seniors, adults with chronic illness, and children and adults with a disability who live on reserve: in-home care, adult foster care and institutional care. Individuals contact their band's assisted living coordinator or band manager to arrange an assessment by a health care provider.
entries.cost_note: Funded by Indigenous Services Canada for people without other means or sources of support; the page does not mention a cost to recipients.
entries.evidence: This program provides funding for non-medical, social support services to seniors, adults with chronic illness, and children and adults with a disability (mental and physical) on reserve to help them maintain their independence.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old servicecanada.gc.ca page; that now lands on the general Service Canada page. The old page redirected to Indigenous and Northern Affairs (archived 2015 copy); the current Indigenous Services Canada page (modified 2022-11-10) describes the same program. Only for people living, or ordinarily resident, on reserve in the provinces and Yukon; NWT and Nunavut residents are covered by territorial programs.

entries.name: A Child’s Voice Foundation
entries.description: A national charity that helps financially disadvantaged children in Canada. Its Angel Hair For Kids program provides wigs and hair-loss solutions, at no cost to the family, to children who lost their hair because of a medical condition or treatment, and Kids Life Line gives one-time help with a needed product or service not covered by health plans or other programs, such as small medical equipment, short-term therapy or transportation to appointments.
entries.cost_note: Angel Hair For Kids wigs are provided at no cost to the child's family; the site does not mention cost for Kids Life Line.
entries.evidence: Angel Hair For Kids is a special program that provides wigs and hair loss solutions to financially disadvantaged children in Canada who have lost their hair due to a medical condition or treatment.
entries.notes: National office in Mississauga, Ontario (contact page). Latest copyright date on the site is 2024. Angel Hair For Kids has an intake form; the Kids Life Line page does not say how to apply.

entries.name: Make-A-Wish Canada
entries.description: Grants wishes to children in Canada aged 3 to 17 who have a critical illness that is currently in the life-threatening stage and who have not had a wish from another wish-granting organization. Parents or legal guardians, the child, or the child's healthcare team can make a referral.
entries.cost_note: The pages do not mention any cost to families.
entries.evidence: We create life-changing wishes for Canadian children with critical illnesses.
entries.notes: CNAF lists it as Children's Wish Foundation (childrenswish.ca); that domain now redirects to makeawish.ca. The eligibility page says autism, ADHD, speech/language delays, learning disabilities, mental health conditions and global developmental delay on their own may not meet its criteria. Contact details from the contact page (office in Toronto).

entries.name: People First of Canada
entries.description: A national, member-led non-profit organization of and for people labelled with an intellectual or developmental disability. Members support each other through peer support, sharing their stories, leadership development and self-advocacy, and it works with provincial and territorial chapters to influence communities and government.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention membership fees.
entries.evidence: People First of Canada is the national organization representing people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
entries.notes: CNAF's link redirects to https://www.peoplefirstofcanada.ca/; the home page says the website is still being rebuilt. National office in Winnipeg (3-120 Maryland Street, about page). Membership is open to people labelled with an intellectual or developmental disability and others listed on the about page. CNAF's People First of Ontario link is dead (see unverified).

entries.name: Autism Service Dogs (National Service Dogs)
entries.description: A registered charity whose certified autism service dogs work with Autistic children and their families: the dog is tethered to the child for safety and takes commands from the parent. Families go through an application and screening process with the charity's social workers, followed by a week of team training.
entries.cost_note: The dog and ongoing support are free, but clients pay a $250 equipment fee, travel and lodging for a week of team training in Kitchener, Ontario, and the dog's day-to-day care.
entries.evidence: Our Certified Service Dogs for Autism increase the safety of children by acting as an anchor when tethered to the child.
entries.notes: Based in Cambridge, Ontario (1286 Cedar Creek Rd.); listed as national because the autism page says it has placed over 622 certified service dogs across Canada. The application process is currently closed; new applicants are taken by referral and quota. Its other programs are for PTSD, canine assisted intervention (Ontario only) and skilled companion dogs.

entries.name: Access 2 Card (Easter Seals Canada)
entries.description: A card for people of any age with a permanent disability who need a support person at participating entertainment, cultural and recreational venues across Canada. The cardholder pays regular admission and one support person gets free or discounted admission; cards are bought for three or five years.
entries.cost_note: There is an administration fee for the card (amount not shown on the pages checked); the support person's admission is free or discounted.
entries.evidence: The Access 2 card is for people of all ages and types of permanent disabilities who require the assistance of a support person at hundreds of participating entertainment, cultural and recreational venues across Canada.
entries.notes: CNAF links to cineplex.com/Theatres/Access2Entertainment, which now redirects to access2card.ca, run by Easter Seals Canada. Processing takes about 4-6 weeks; the Toronto office serves people in person by appointment only.

entries.name: Disability Travel Card (Easter Seals Canada)
entries.description: A card for people with a permanent disability who need a support person when travelling with VIA Rail Canada: the cardholder pays the regular fare and one support person can travel with them at a reduced fare. A health care professional or recognized service provider must complete part of the application; the card does not expire and is not valid with airlines.
entries.cost_note: The application form does not mention a fee for the card; the support person travels at a reduced fare.
entries.evidence: The Disability Travel Card is for people of all types of permanent disabilities who require the assistance of a support person when travelling with VIA Rail Canada.
entries.notes: CNAF links to the 2023 application form (PDF), which also names Coach Canada; the current Easter Seals Canada programs page names only VIA Rail Canada. On VIA Rail the card cannot be used for children under 8. Processing takes about 4 weeks.

entries.name: Easter Seals Canada
entries.description: A national charity for people with disabilities that runs national programs such as the Access 2 Card and the Disability Travel Card and supports the provincial Easter Seals organizations, which deliver local programs such as camps, assistive equipment funding, recreation and respite. Programs vary from province to province, and the site links to the Easter Seals organization in each province.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention cost; programs differ by province.
entries.evidence: Easter Seals Canada is a federated organization, with provincial offices representing all provinces and territories.
entries.notes: CNAF's link easterseals.ca/english/ redirects to easterseals.ca/en/. National office in Toronto (40 Holly St, Suite 401). The Access 2 Card and Disability Travel Card are separate entries; Easter Seals Ontario equipment funding is already in scripts/data/services/funding.json as easter-seals-ontario-equipment-funding.

entries.name: Learning Disabilities Association of Canada (LDAC)
entries.description: A national charity that supports people with learning disabilities, promotes inclusive practices and advocates for equal opportunities. For help with assessments, tools and resources, it refers parents and adults to the Learning Disabilities Association in their province or territory, which it lists with contact details.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention cost.
entries.evidence: There is a Learning Disabilities Association (LDA) located in nine provinces and one territory across Canada and from these extends a network of chapters in more than 30 communities across the country.
entries.notes: CNAF's link redirects to https://www.ldac-acta.ca/. Office in Ottawa (about page). Several local LDA programs in Ontario are already in scripts/data/services/nd_mentoring.json (for example lda-toronto-smart-kidz-tutoring).

entries.name: Autism Awareness Centre Inc.
entries.description: A Calgary-based company that runs autism conferences and trainings across Canada, live and recorded webinars, and a bookstore of autism resources for parents and professionals. It also publishes free articles and a list of autism help and resources by region, and offers Studio 3 Low Arousal Approach training on managing behaviour.
entries.cost_note: Books, webinars and conferences are sold through the site and an order form; articles and the newsletter subscription are free.
entries.evidence: Autism Awareness Centre hosts trainings across Canada, while ensuring books, articles and resource supports are readily available to all communities keeping parents and professionals on the cutting edge of new information.
entries.notes: CNAF's link autismawarenesscentre.org redirects to autismawarenesscentre.com. Office in Calgary, Alberta (56 Sussex Crescent SW); listed as national because its trainings and webinars are offered across Canada. The only email shown is the director's own address, so none is given; the about page was last updated October 13, 2022.

entries.name: Canadian Association of Music Therapists (CAMT)
entries.description: National non-profit professional association for Certified Music Therapists (MTA). Its site explains music therapy, lists the provincial and regional music therapy associations, and has a directory to check whether someone is a Certified Music Therapist.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention cost for the public.
entries.evidence: The Canadian Association of Music Therapists (CAMT) is a federally incorporated, self-regulated non-profit professional association dedicated to fostering the practice of music therapy in clinical, educational, and community settings throughout Canada.
entries.notes: CNAF links to CAMT's French home page inside its Quebec listing for the AQM. The site gives an office address in Vancouver (303-2346 W 43rd Ave.) and a registered address in Ottawa. The "charity" tag reflects the site's "non-profit" wording.

entries.name: Cybertip.ca (Canadian Centre for Child Protection)
entries.description: Cybertip.ca is Canada's national tipline, run by the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, for reporting the online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, such as online luring and the sharing of intimate images of anyone under 18. It takes reports online or by phone, refers leads to police or child welfare, and offers information, support and referrals to help families stay safe online.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention cost.
entries.evidence: Cybertip.ca is Canada’s tipline for reporting the online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.
entries.notes: CNAF's link (cybertip.ca/app/en/report) redirects to the current report page. The tipline works 8:30am to 4:00pm Central Time, Monday to Friday; for a child in immediate danger the site says to call 9-1-1. Phone from the Contact page. CNAF lists it as a place to report cyberbullying that may be a crime; it handles online sexual exploitation of children, not bullying in general.

entries.name: Inclusive Education Canada (IEC)
entries.description: Inclusive Education Canada, an initiative of Inclusion Canada, advocates for schools across Canada where students with intellectual and other disabilities learn alongside their peers with the support they need. Its website gives parents, educators and communities information, news and guides on inclusive education and the right to education.
entries.cost_note: The site does not mention cost.
entries.evidence: Inclusive Education Canada (IEC) advocates for equitable and inclusive education across Canada, ensuring every student, regardless of ability, has the support and opportunities they need to succeed.
entries.notes: CNAF links to https://inclusiveeducation.ca/learn/right-to-education/, which now returns 404; the same topic is at https://www.inclusiveeducation.ca/right-to-education. IEC (est. 2002) is an information and advocacy group rather than a direct service; contact details from its Contact page (head office Toronto, mailing address Oshawa), and the email is the organisation's own address.

entries.name: The Hanen Centre
entries.description: A Toronto-based not-for-profit that develops parent programs to build young children's language and social communication skills, run in small in-person or online groups by speech-language pathologists it trains and certifies. Its More Than Words program is for parents of young autistic children, and another program is for parents of autistic children aged 4 to 8; the site helps families find a Hanen-certified SLP and has free articles and tips.
entries.cost_note: The site does not list program fees (programs are run by Hanen-certified SLPs); articles and tips are free to read and guidebooks are sold in its shop.
entries.address: 110 Eglinton Avenue East Suite 601 Toronto, ON Canada, M4P 2Y1
entries.evidence: Hanen Programs are offered by speech-language pathologists (SLPs) around the world who’ve received special training and certification from The Hanen Centre™.
entries.notes: National (and international) resource: programs are led by Hanen-certified SLPs wherever families live, in person or online, so it is placed in national entries. The Hanen Centre does not run therapy itself; families find a certified SLP through its site. Address and phone from the contact page (contact form, no public email).

entries.name: Embrace Autism
entries.description: An autistic-led organization that offers online autism and AuDHD screenings and full diagnostic assessments for adults (18+), carried out by licensed psychologists, including autistic psychologists, with experience assessing late-identified and high-masking adults. It also publishes free articles, tests and resources for autistic adults and offers post-diagnostic support.
entries.cost_note: An autism screening assessment costs CA$625 and an autism diagnostic assessment CA$1,895 (as listed on its assessments page).
entries.evidence: Formal autism assessments offered through Embrace Autism are conducted by licensed psychologists, including autistic psychologists, with experience assessing autism in adults, including late-identified and high-masking autistic adults.
entries.notes: CNAF links to an old page about Dr. Natalie Engelbrecht on embrace-autism.com, which now redirects to a 404 page; the organisation's current site is embrace-autism.com. Online only: its land acknowledgement refers to Ontario, and its psychologists are in Canada, the US, Australia and elsewhere, with the assessor depending on where the client lives, so a reviewer may decide whether it belongs in national entries. No phone or email is published (contact form only). Moved to national: it works online and serves people across Canada.
